what: Sommelier V1+ P8: free quality measurement and performance benchmarks of the integrated build (commit 0fc8c09, the merge of P2-P7). No model was called, nothing was sent, no key was used; the v1-ai engine was not run.
machine: 4 shared cores (Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz), Node 22; other agents were running on the same machine (load average 9.3 at the start of the latency run, 1.5 at its end; 25 minutes). Wall-clock numbers are this machine on this day, not production.

latency.how: createSommelierService as server/services.ts wires it, a fake model that answers at once with a fixed realistic answer (3 bottle_refs for a pairing, one course entry per course for a menu when the schema asks for courses, the named wine for a serving question), in-memory reads, generated cellars (bench-cellar.ts). Per cell: 20 warm-up rounds, then 200 measured rounds, every configuration once per round in a rotating order. p50/p95/max of the wall clock of one ask; delta = configuration minus V1 (or minus V1 without a model) in the same cell. Percentile as score.ts: the value at floor(p*n).

questions.pairing-guests: We are 6 for dinner tonight: roast lamb with rosemary and garlic. Which bottle should I open? (a pairing with a guest count, so quantities has work)
questions.menu-3: Oysters to start, then roast lamb, and for dessert chocolate fondant. Which wine with each course?
questions.serving: How should I serve the Vajrelli, and should I decant it? (names one cellar wine by its producer)

summary.over300Ms: all five together at 3,000 wines: menu-3 +891.6 / +855.3 ms (1 / 12 messages), serving +380.3 / +364.3 ms, pairing-guests +304.9 ms (12 messages); pairing-guests with 1 message +274.8 ms. At 500 wines the worst is +134.9 ms (all, menu-3); at 120 wines +24.2 ms; at 25 wines +5.7 ms.
summary.whereTheTimeGoes: checkAnswerClaims indexes the whole cellar on every call (p50 0.8 / 3.5 / 21 / 176 ms at 25 / 120 / 500 / 3,000 wines, `components`); with check and menu both on it runs once for the answer and once more for each course's reason, so a 3-course menu at 3,000 wines pays it four times. The serving facts (annotate) read the whole cellar to find the named wine (p50 90 ms at 3,000). menu's compareRequest/menuContext add up to ~60 ms at 3,000 wines on a question that names wines.
summary.profileReadsPerAsk: at most 1 with annotate (or with the fallback on the no-model path), 0 otherwise: measured, not assumed. In-memory here; in production one round trip to vintage_insights.
summary.noModelPath: V1 without a model: p95 up to 147 ms at 3,000 wines (the plain pairing engine). With fallback: within -14 / +6.2 ms of it in every cell.

cost.how: The request the service builds for one ask, recorded before the fake model answers. promptChars = system + user + JSON schema (as paid.ts estimating() counts). inputTokens = ceil(chars/3). maxOutputTokens after planCall. highMicro = pricing.ts estimateCost (input + full output allowance, two attempts). reservationMicro = paid.ts reservationFor. typicalMicro = one attempt, input + a typical output (180 tokens, +45 per course for a planned menu; an assumption, not measured). vsV1 = percent change against V1 (prompt v6, no part) for the same question, conversation and cellar. The cellar list is capped at 120 wines (DIGEST_MAX), so 120 and 3000 wines give nearly the same prompt.

evalSets.how: Every scenario V1 can attempt (needs within pairing, facts) asked turn by turn through the service with the parts on and paid.ts estimating() as the model; the V1 row equals the repo's own `pnpm sommelier:eval --engine v1-ai --estimate --set main --needs pairing,facts` (131 calls, 340,592 tokens in, $0.2031).

rows.config: all (no fallback: it adds no call)
all (no fallback: it adds no call)
all (no fallback: it adds no call)

commands: SOMMELIER_EVAL_BLIND_SALT=<the P7 salt, never committed> pnpm sommelier:eval --engine <v1-fallback|v1-basic> --set <main|holdout-dev|holdout-test> --vectors <outside the repository>/<set>-<engine>.json
fallback.result: Reproduced exactly on 0fc8c09: every per-scenario vector of v1-fallback and v1-basic equals the committed p7 vectors (main 146 and 124, holdout-dev 45 and 45; holdout-test 43 and 43 compared under the same salt, reported in totals only), and every difference and 95% interval equals p7-fallback.json to 4 decimals. fallback.test.ts passes.
fallback.note: The v1-fallback engine calls createSommelierFallback directly and then the service with llm = null; it does not go through the service's own fallback wiring (deps.parts + deps.fallback). fallback-wired.ts plays every scenario both ways (the engine's way, and the integrated service with parts = fallback and deps.fallback set, llm = null): the last answers are identical for main 246/246, holdout-dev 45/45 and holdout-test 43/43 (totals only). Tested in bench.test.ts.

commands: pnpm sommelier:eval --engine v1-basic --set <set> --vectors <file> (in a worktree of 0fc8c09 and one of origin/main b13cf26; the blind set with the P7 salt)
pnpm sommelier:eval --engine v1-basic --set <main|holdout-dev> --json <file> (per-scenario pass/fail of all scenarios, compared field by field)
v1Unchanged.result: v1-basic gives identical per-scenario vectors on 0fc8c09 and origin/main (b13cf26) for all three sets: main 124/124, holdout-dev 45/45, holdout-test 43/43 (blind, salted keys). The per-scenario results (pass and failed checks) of all 246 main and 45 holdout-dev scenarios are identical too, as are labels and measures; the holdout-test totals report is identical apart from the latency line.

annotationSample.command: pnpm --filter @cellr/sommelier-eval run annotation-sample --write, then pnpm prettier --write on the file
annotationSample.note: NOT reviewed by any person. 49 of 50 rows carry a lowest-confidence flag from the code itself (serving by rule of thumb for the style or the colour, or a window estimated for the style); one row (a wine with a researched profile) is stated as known for that wine.

menu.scorer: menu-score.ts scoreMenu/scoreCourse: per course right / acceptable / poor against menuExpectations (the dish cards' AI-written labels). Tested on synthetic answers and end to end through the service with a model that picks the labelled right wines (18/18 menus, every course right) and one that picks poor wines.
menu.estimateNote: One call per turn (18 menus, 21 turns). Nothing was sent: paid.ts estimating() answers 'unavailable' and the service gives its plain answer, so the follow-up turns carry '…' as the earlier answer; a paid run would carry the model's words (up to 400 characters each in the history), about 3 x 400 characters more in all.

gate.note: Thresholds are the closeout's proposals (D-50), not owner decisions. 'Free' means without a model.
gate.firstBottleRight_noPoorBottle_usefulAnsw: NOT MEASURABLE FREE: needs the paid v1-ai baseline and V1+ run (owner's budget approval, D-51).
gate.inventedBottleVintageFact: Not measurable free for answers with a model. Free paths: v1-fallback invents 0 bottles on all three sets (fallback.test.ts); the fake-model harness cannot test it (the fake is well-behaved).
gate.unverifiedPriceShopStock: Not measurable free for answers with a model. Free path: v1-fallback gives no buying advice or price on all three sets.
gate.annotationCorrectness: Fixtures: the repo's unit tests pass (pnpm test). Sample of 50: GENERATED, NOT REVIEWED (results/p4-annotation-sample.md). NOT MET until a person reviews it.
gate.latency: Part overhead only (fake model, in-memory reads). MET for every part alone at every cellar size (worst +252 ms, check at 3,000 wines) and for all five together up to 500 wines (worst +135 ms). NOT MET for all five together at 3,000 wines: +305 to +892 ms on four of six cells (worst: a 3-course menu, check runs per course). Whether the eval run's cellars (2-30 wines) meet it: yes, by a wide margin (+6 ms at 25 wines); the real p95 with a model must still be measured in the paid run.
gate.cost: Prompt and output allowance, free estimate. MET for every non-menu question: high estimate +1.1 to +5.2% (all parts), prompt characters up to +13% (all parts, 25 wines, serving); on the eval sets main / holdout-dev / holdout-test: +2.3 / +2.4 / +2.4% high estimate (+5.5 to +6.1% characters), check being the only part that changes their prompts. NOT MET on a worst-case basis for a NEW MENU: the output allowance grows 70 tokens a course (900 -> 1110 for 3 courses, 1460 for 8), so the high estimate is +12.8% (3 courses) and +28.2% (8 courses) with menu alone at 120 wines, +43.3% / +45.7% (menu / all) for 8 courses at 25 wines; the input alone is +6 to +9% at 120 wines but +14 to +21% at 25 wines. Over the 18-menu set: +17.2% high estimate (+13.6% prompt characters) with menu on, +19.6% (+19.6%) with check and menu. A menu question is a rare share of all questions; per answer on the menu it exceeds +10%.
gate.fallbackVsPlain: Reproduced on 0fc8c09: MET on main and holdout-test (lower bounds +24 / +14 first bottle, +51 / +35 no poor bottle); holdout-dev first bottle lower bound +0, NOT STRICTLY MET (as in P7).

limitations: Fake model: answers at once with a fixed, well-formed answer that follows the prompt (refs as [[ref]] under v7). Real models take seconds, write other words (which changes what check does and how long it takes) and sometimes fail; the measured numbers are the overhead of the app's own code only.
In-memory reads: the cellar, profiles, taste and Tonight reads cost nothing here. The parts add at most one profiles read per ask (measured); its database round trip is not in the numbers.

Shared CPU: 4 cores shared with other agents (load average 9.3 at the start, 1.5 at the end of the latency run). Configurations were interleaved round by round so a slow moment falls on all; absolute times are this machine on this day.

Generated cellars: realistic in shape but invented (bench-cellar.ts); real cellars differ in names, which changes the cost of the name-matching rules. The eval's own fixture ids are counted (refs 32 characters instead of 6), so the eval-set cost estimates err high in absolute terms for every configuration alike; the bench cellars use random-looking ids.

Cost is an estimate: characters/3 as tokens and the full output allowance (pricing.ts estimateCost); the typical-output column assumes 180 tokens (+45 a course), not measured. No provider bill was read.

AI-written labels: the dish cards behind the eval sets and the menu set were written by an AI and reviewed by nobody who knows wine (R-01, R-11). The fallback numbers and the menu scorer inherit that.
The menu estimate's follow-up turns carry '…' as the earlier answer (nothing was sent), up to about 1,200 history characters less than a paid run.
The annotation sample has not been reviewed by a person; its flags are the code's own bases, not a judgement.

In the serving question the wine is named by its producer only ('the Vajrelli'): with 'the Vajrelli Barolo', the serving facts match every Barolo by name and give no block once more than three match (FACTS_WINES_MAX), as P4-P5 documents; in the 120+ wine cellars that is the usual case.
